#3279. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

Peeling paint, bubbling wallpaper, mold behind wardrobes, and water-stained ceilings — I’ve seen all the classic signs of excess moisture in my own home.

But while window condensation is an obvious telltale sign of too much moisture inside my house, the root cause of the other issues isn’t so clear.

But before calling in a specialist, there’s a simple test you can try to determine whether the moisture is coming from inside or out.

Beyond covering your Thanksgiving turkey, aluminum foil can help with a stack of hacks around your home, including identifying which sides of your walls are holding excess moisture.

All you need to do is take a piece of aluminum foil and tape it to your wall. Within 48 hours, it should give you an indication of where the moisture is coming from.

But how does this aluminum foil hack work, and is it reliable? Michael Rubino, mold and air quality expert at HomeCleanse, explains: “Aluminum foil doesn’t allow water vapor to pass through it easily, because it’s a non-porous surface. When you tape it against a wall, you’re essentially blocking moisture from moving between that section of the wall and the air in the room.”

And he adds, “If the air inside your home is humid and the foil gets cool enough, that moisture in the air can condense into water droplets on the side facing the room.”

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The same process happens when you spot condensation on the inside of your windows.

However, what if the moisture is coming from the wall? Rubino explains, “If there is already moisture in the wall, that moisture would normally have some opportunity to evaporate into the room as the material dries. Covering it with foil, prevents that from happening in that particular spot. In this case, moisture collects behind the foil instead.”

Rubino explains that checking which side of the aluminum foil is wet can tell you something about how moisture is behaving in that exact area. But it can’t tell you exactly where that water came from.

If you remove the foil and find moisture against the wall, you might assume rainwater is getting in from outside, but he says that’s only one possibility. “A pipe could be leaking inside the wall, or water could be entering through the foundation.”

He explains that other possibilities include water entering through the foundation or condensation forming inside the wall cavity due to high humidity or poor insulation.

It's also possible you have more than one moisture issue at once. Rubino explains, “If you find water droplets on the side facing the room, that doesn’t mean you’ve ruled out a leak behind the wall, either.”

Dr. Alex Le Beau, a toxicologist and environmental scientist at Exposure Consulting, says a visual assessment is a good way to start checking whether moisture has entered your home, and professionals will do this too.

He explains that wet building material, such as a drywall, within the built environment is not normal, and that the location of the moisture should be the first thing to note — is it on an exterior or interior wall or the ceiling?

He also advises looking at the pattern it is making. Depending on the material, he says, "It will take a good amount of water to soak through the back of something. Soaking like this may make the material brittle to the touch or could cause surface deformations."

Dr. Le Beau says to look out for paint bubbling or staining coming through from the back of the material.

Internal condensation may also look different. He says, “There may be a pattern to the moisture from internal humidity, or it may form at the same spot and then evaporate when internal conditioning (HVAC) begins to cycle."

While a dry sheet of aluminum foil on your wall may seem like a good sign, Rubino warns against using a single piece of information to judge your home’s condition. "There’s too much it can’t account for, and a dry result doesn’t mean you’re in the clear,” he says.

Another of Rubino’s concerns about this hack is that it can’t be used to detect mold. "You could find moisture behind the foil and have no idea whether mold has started growing inside the wall,” he says.

It also won’t determine how much of the surrounding area is affected or whether contamination has spread beyond that area.

He’s also found that the opposite can be true. "I’ve seen plenty of situations where the original water problem happened months or even years earlier,” he says, “The material may have dried out since then, but that doesn't mean any mold growth that developed during that time has disappeared as well."

While the aluminum foil hack can give you an idea of what’s happening on your walls, it doesn’t give you a definitive answer. And that’s why Rubino says it’s important to understand the entire situation and to ask questions: where has the moisture come from, how long has it been there, what materials have been affected, and has microbial growth developed?

“A piece of foil isn't going to answer all those questions, and those are the answer you really need if you’re concerned about the health of your home," he explains.

And he adds, “If you notice discoloration around a window, a musty smell that keeps coming back, or an area that never seems to dry completely, don’t just paint over it or assume it’s nothing. Find out what’s causing it.”

The sooner you understand what’s going on, the better your chances of addressing the problem before the damage becomes more extensive.

#3275. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3274. iOS 27.2 adds three new ways to customize your iPhone

iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization.

Inside Settings ⇾ Siri there’s a new ‘Excluded Apps’ section in iOS 27.2. This makes it easier than ever to remove certain apps from being accessible to Siri, Search, and more. Apple says:

Apps added to the list below will be excluded from Siri, Search, and suggestions.

iOS 27.2 adds a new Messages feature called Suggestions that I’m a big fan of. When relevant content is detected in a conversation, you might see a Suggestion appear underneath a message. For example, if a friend asks you to do them a favor, you might see “Add to Reminders” below the message.

By default there are five supported categories of Suggestions:

You can fully customize these to your own preferences and needs. Just go to Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions to disable whichever Suggestions you don’t want to see.

Historically, Apple TV has only ever supported user profiles on tvOS. It’s an odd limitation considering every other streaming service offers profiles across platforms.

But finally with iOS 27.2, profiles are now available on iPhone too, letting you customize the content in the Apple TV app based on who’s watching.

Choosing a profile not only gives you personalized recommendations from Apple TV, it also lets you keep the ‘Continue Watching’ queue separate for each person. And if you’re setting up a profile for a child, you can set content restrictions too.

#3272. Orion Energy (OESX) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

LED lighting growth offset EV charging weakness this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Orion Energy Systems, Inc. (OESX -7.67%) reported a 9% revenue increase for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and reiterated its recently upgraded full-year revenue guidance. Management attributed the growth primarily to the LED Lighting segment, which offset declines in EV charging and maintenance revenue. The company reported its eighth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA, supported by increased project activity with major retail and data center customers. Financial performance in the quarter was influenced by a mix shift that temporarily lowered gross margins, though management expects these rates to return to levels above 30% in the second half of the year.

Operator: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Orion Energy Systems' Fiscal 2027 Second Quarter Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] In this call, Sally Washlow, Orion's CEO; and Per Brodin, its CFO, will review the company's second quarter results as well as its fiscal 2027 outlook. Then we will open the call to investors' questions. [Operator Instructions] Today's call is being recorded. A replay will be posted in the Investors section of the company's website, orionlighting.com. I will now turn the call over to Per Brodin, Orion's CFO.

John Brodin: Thank you, Corey. First, as a reminder, prepared remarks and answers to questions on this call include statements that are forward-looking under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements generally include words such as anticipate, believe, expect, project or similar words. Also, any statements describing future objectives or goals, company plans and outlook are also forward-looking. These forward-looking statements are subject to various risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from current expectations. Risks include, among other matters, those that Orion has described in its press release issued this morning and in its SEC filings. Except as described therein, Orion disclaims any obligation to update or revise forward-looking statements made as of today.

In addition, reconciliations of certain non-GAAP financial metrics to their nearest GAAP measures are also provided in today's press release. And now I will turn the call over to Orion's CEO, Sally Washlow.

Sally Washlow: Thank you, Per. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for being with us today. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, we delivered growth of 9% year-over-year. All of Orion's business segments, LED Lighting, EV charging and Maintenance recorded expected levels of financial performance in the second quarter and continue on a trajectory to meet our full fiscal year guidance. As a reminder, those expectations, which we recently increased are to achieve positive adjusted EBITDA on revenue of between $100 million and $102 million, an increase from prior guidance of $95 million to $97 million in FY '27.

As we head into the second half of the fiscal year, FY '27 shapes up as a continuation of the successful turnaround we began in FY 2026, which came in at $86 million in revenue and $2 million in positive adjusted EBITDA. FY '26 represented a return to growth for this company in both revenue and profitability. Orion's unrivaled supply chain and project management capabilities are attributes that I cannot emphasize enough. Our resilient supply chain provides a competitive advantage that is consistently cited by Orion's customers.

Many of our customers come back to Orion asking to expand the work we are doing with them, whether it is expanding the scope of work at a single facility or adding increased opportunities at additional locations. These projects run the gamut ranging from lighting only to EV infrastructure projects to electrical contracting. Our existing expectations for this fiscal year reflect our confidence in the continuing growth trajectory for the company, along with recent industry research that informs us that we are about to begin a new industrial LED lighting replacement cycle.

The October cover story of a respected industry publication, Lighting Management & Maintenance, reports that 10% to 20% of America's LED installed base may already be due for replacement. For commercial, industrial and outdoor applications, the segment that Orion serves, that replacement cycle may be 20% to 30%. Orion's recent announcements serve as early indicators of this replacement cycle. As for FY '27 specifically, the quarter included a number of milestones. Q2 marked an additional multimillion deployment of our data center lighting solution for one of the world's largest hyperscalers. This followed June's announcement of our first multimillion-dollar deployment for this globally renowned hyperscaler.

We believe we are still in the early innings of deploying our cost-saving and energy-efficient solution with this hyperscaler, and there is still growth in this segment, evidenced by our discussions of finalizing additional scope to our already announced wins. Our customizable lighting solution manufactured right here in Wisconsin is capable of delivering higher energy efficiency, resiliency and decarbonization in LED lighting. Another announcement, our latest $10 million to $15 million engagement with a major nationwide retailer. Our long-time customer made a follow-on commitment to us in the second quarter for a new LED lighting project estimated to represent $10 million to $15 million.

We believe we will achieve the higher range of this commitment, and we will keep you apprised as we execute this project in Q3 and Q4. This latest scope of work involves retrofitting interior LED lighting and IoT system installations at locations we had not previously retrofitted. This is the most recent in a multiyear sequence of engagements for us with this well-known brand. Furthermore, we believe this will expand to additional stores, which could equal or be more than our previously announced project. We've seen adoption of the full spectrum of Orion's products and services, typified by our recent announcement of a global automotive leader that is deploying both our LED lighting solutions and our EV charging infrastructure.

We will continue to focus on scaling EV charging across a broader customer base and geographic footprint. More than ever, industrial America requires full-footprint LED lighting, EV charging and electrical infrastructure. It needs it at scale and at the maximum of efficiency and cost effectiveness. We believe strongly that we will continue to be a provider of choice for AI and IoT-driven electrification to Fortune 100 corporations and other global leaders. With that, let me turn it over to Orion's CFO, Per Brodin, to review our financial performance and outlook.

John Brodin: Thank you, Sally. Today, we reported fiscal Q2 '27 revenue of $21.7 million compared to $19.9 million in Q2 '26. LED Lighting segment revenue in Q2 '27 was $14.9 million compared to $10.7 million in Q2 '26. Q2 '27 Lighting segment revenue performance reflected increased project activity and distribution channel sales, partially offset by a decrease in ESCO channel sales. Orion's expanded LED lighting project pipeline and efforts to drive growth in the distribution channel are continuing to contribute to improving performance in fiscal '27. Lighting achieved a Q2 '27 gross margin of 29.1% versus 27.5% in Q2 '26. Maintenance segment revenue was $4 million in Q2 '27 compared to $4.5 million in Q2 '26.

We achieved a Maintenance segment gross margin of 25.3% in Q2 '27 versus 23.7% in Q2 '26. EV charging solutions revenue was $2.8 million in Q2 '27 compared to $4.8 million in Q2 '26, reflecting a year-over-year reduction in project volume. EV achieved a gross margin of 31.4% in Q2 '27 versus 45.8% in Q2 '26. Our overall gross profit margin was 28.7% in Q2 '27 versus 31% in Q2 '26. The Q2 '27 margin decrease was largely driven by a mix shift within the Lighting segment. We expect our margin rate to normalize back to the 30-plus percent neighborhood in Q3 and Q4. Total operating expenses were $7 million in Q2 '27 compared to $6.4 million in Q2 '26.

Increases in stock-based compensation and general and administrative expenses, along with increased commission expense included in sales and marketing costs were the main drivers of the increase. Reflecting lower gross margin and higher operating expenses, Orion's Q2 '27 net loss was $0.8 million or $0.20 per share compared to a net loss of $0.6 million or $0.17 per share in Q2 '26. Adjusted EBITDA was positive in Q2 '27 and was $0.5 million in Q2 '26. As Sally pointed out, this was Orion's eighth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA. Regarding our outlook, as Sally highlighted, we expect a continued increase in profitable growth in fiscal '27, with positive adjusted EBITDA and revenue between $100 million and $102 million.

Given the remaining revenue needed to achieve this guidance, we expect both Q3 and Q4 revenue to be relatively even. Any upside mentioned by Sally would occur in Q4. And this concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, would you please commence the question-and-answer session?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Sameer Joshi of H.C. Wainwright.

Sameer Joshi: Congrats on the upgraded guidance. That was good to see. So on the hyperscaler wins that you are experiencing, how should we look at these? Are these for unique sites? Or are these for a set of sites? And what is the strategy going forward or rather the sales cycle going forward where do you expect the same hyperscalers to contract you for additional sites?

Sally Washlow: Yes. Thanks for the question. We expect with this hyperscaler, and as we've said earlier, how we've won is we first get approved on their campuses to install or to sell our lighting fixtures. We're not doing the installation. And then we win building by building. And each building is 7 figures of lighting fixtures alone. So we've won 2, and we're in discussions of another building as well that we expect to come shortly. So there's a lot of noise in data centers.

But with the hyperscaler that we're working with and the locations that we're in, we think that they're going to continue to grow, and we're in the early innings with this hyperscaler on the amount of buildings that we'll be able to win with them and then share the solution with others as well.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And as far as the products that they want, is there any -- are you learning of new specifications that may need upgrade to your products, new products being offered to these hyperscalers in particular?

Sally Washlow: If you're looking at it from a lens of retrofitting data centers, not anything in our line of sight. This is with new buildings that have already been announced and in flight, in construction of these data centers.

Sameer Joshi: Okay. On the EV sort of Voltrek and deployment at automakers, how is that sales process? Is it that the EV team gets the lead and they also get a lighting contract? Or is it the other way around where you are doing a lighting job and then EV gets invited?

Sally Washlow: So the good news is it's starting to work both ways. With the global automotive maker, it was a lighting project that we are doing, and then they brought the EV team in to help with that solution, in particular, and then we won EV charging at that one site. And quite frankly, we're looking at a couple of other sites with them as well. There are some other opportunities where the EV team has been in and looked at their lighting solutions and then are bringing our lighting team in to recommend solutions. So we are seeing more collaboration and a bit more opportunities in cross-selling between the 2 segments.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And then just a couple of sort of financial questions. Given that at least the 2Q -- fiscal 2Q service revenue was lower, should we expect the annual mix of product versus service to skew even more towards product revenues? And a corollary of that is if that happens, should we expect gross margins -- blended gross margins to be higher, relatively higher?

John Brodin: I think as we expect the rest of the fiscal year to play out, it likely will skew a little bit more toward product based on the projects that are underway. But I wouldn't call that a markedly significant change. And as I mentioned in my comments, we do expect our margin rate to, call it, normalize back to 30-plus where it's been most recently, because we did have a mix shift change that simply impacted Q2 of this year.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And then last one on accounts payable. I think, quarter-over-quarter, almost -- a little over $5 million in drop. Was there anything specific that happened there? Or is it just timing?

John Brodin: It's primarily timing. It really goes to the working capital investment we've talked about for some of these more significant projects.

Gowshihan Sriharan: Hope you can all hear me?

Gowshihan Sriharan: On the [indiscernible] grows, how much are you doing with your own crews versus subcontractors? And how have the subcontractor rates moved over the past year?

Gowshihan Sriharan: Okay. And I'll just sneak in the last one. The purchase order on the interior projects, how are they flowing so far? How does the margin on the interior work compare with kind of your exterior programs?

Sally Washlow: And the timing, as we've said, is Q3 and Q4.

John Brodin: Yes. Maybe one thing I'd add since we didn't comment on this, in the 10-Q, you will see that our backlog at the end of September sits at about $21.6 million or $21.7 million. Luke Persons: This is Luke on for Eric. So I guess, first here on the data center, how have you leveraged your successes with this initial customer and the engagements with other potential data center customers? Is your distribution partner continuing to help you penetrate this market? And also, would you ever consider going to a direct sales model down the road in this market?

Sally Washlow: So our distribution partner with the hyperscaler that we're working with, we do plan to discuss with others within that partner. #3271. HomeKit Weekly: Airversa’s Humelle is the Thread humidifier my house needs this winter

I love natural gas heat for a few reasons, but one is avoiding AUX heat from a heat pump and watching the bill rise. The downside is when the gas heat kicks on, the air in mt house is bone dry. My nose ends up being super dry for months. A humidifier like the Airversa Humelle works with Apple Home over Thread, so it can run itself based on what the air actually needs, and with the temps in my area getting into the 40s in the next week, I am glad I have one.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Airversa Humelle humidifier uses Thread, so it does join your existing Thread network via a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K and communicates with Apple Home locally. In my experience, Thread accessories always respond faster and drop connections less than Wi-Fi-only ones, and they don’t add to the pile of devices fighting for airtime on your router either. Especially since most smart home devices are 2.4 GHz only.

Once the Airversa Humelle is paired with Apple Home, it appears in the Home app as a humidifier with a built-in temperature and humidity sensor. The latter sensor is the key for automations as well. You can set a target humidity level, and in Auto Mode, it ramps the mist up or down on its own to hold that number. For most people, that’s all the automation they’ll ever need. Set it to 45%, and it’ll run forever. By including that sensor in the device, you don’t need to pair it with a separate Apple Home-compatible humidity sensor for the automations. In fact, that is probably the only automation to run with this device.

The Humelle has a 3.2L tank that Airversa rates at up to 60 hours of runtime, and the mist reaches about 40 inches high, so it covers a bedroom or an average-sized living room pretty easily. It’s a top-fill design, which honestly is the only way these should be made at this point. Flipping them over always ends with some water on the floor.

Sleep Mode runs at 28dB, which is good for a baby’s room, etc. There’s a multicolor LED on the base that you can set to whatever color you want from the Home app or the Sleekpoint app, or turn off completely. There’s also a tray for essential oils if you want it to double as a diffuser to improve a room’s smell.

One thing to know about the Airversa Humelle going in: you’ll still want the Sleekpoint app for a few things, like setting a cleaning reminder that pings you when it’s time to rinse the tank. Day-to-day control lives in Apple Home, but the setup and maintenance features live in the manufacturer’s app. That’s just where Matter is as a protocol right now.

Natural gas heat dries out your inside air, and the Airversa Humelle fixes it. It allows me to avoid regretting my heating choice when I built my house. A humidifier that knows when the air is dry and turns on is the secret sauce. The Humelle does that in Apple Home with Thread, giving you a humidity sensor you can build the rest of your winter automations around. If you need a Thread Border Router, one of the new HomePod mini 2 units is the best to get started.

The Airversa Humelle is available on Amazon and directly from Airversa.
